query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A staged high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment forms a stable, adherent oxide layer on as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings that significantly reduces wear by limiting metal–metal contact and impeding both abrasive and adhesive failure mechanisms at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited sputtered FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a staged high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment (e.g., heating to 800–900°C for a defined duration) to induce controlled oxide layer formation.
generation.conditions: Wear testing conducted over a temperature range from room temperature up to 800–900°C under incremental loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, uniformly adherent oxide layer (potentially a spinel or mixed oxide) that acts as a physical barrier.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide minimizes direct metal contact and reduces friction by serving as a protective barrier, thereby curbing wear rates under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to as-deposited controls, pre-oxidized coatings will display lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates, as confirmed by smoother wear track morphologies and more intact oxide layers observed post-test.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coatings with no oxidation pre-treatment.
generation.boundary: The expected benefits are restricted to high-temperature wear conditions (above 500°C up to 900°C) and may not extend to extreme thermal regimes where oxide layers could spall or the coating’s integrity could be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxide composition, its thickness, and adhesion quality—and how these parameters quantitatively correlate with wear resistance across the temperature range—require further detailed characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on the same substrate: one subjected to the staged high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment and one left as-deposited. Perform reciprocating wear tests across a temperature range from room temperature to 900°C under controlled, incremental loading conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss)
Surface morphology and wear track characterization (using SEM/EDS)
Phase identification and oxide layer integrity (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower wear rates and reduced COF) compared to the as-deposited control, or if the oxide layer is found to be discontinuous or non-adherent under high-temperature wear conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Studies of high-entropy alloy coatings for wear have so far established that complex compositions benefit from oxide or compound-layer formation at high temperatures, improving tribological performance. Early work focused on AlCoCrFeNi-based coatings up to 900 °C (PMC7515071), revealing that temperature-induced spinel formation significantly enhanced wear resistance. Parallel efforts with refractory thin films (PMC7304825) demonstrated enhanced adhesion and lowered friction up to moderate temperatures (300 °C) but did not examine broader high-temperature regimes or FeNiCrCoCu compositions. Synthesis and testing methods varied (powder metallurgy vs. sputtered films), indicating that multi-temperature, systematic evaluations for FeNiCrCoCu protective coatings remain underexplored.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how FeNiCrCoCu coatings respond to wear across a wide temperature range, especially above 500 °C, and whether a persistent, protective surface oxide or another phase stabilizes their frictional and wear behavior at high temperatures.
decision.lever: Implement a staged, high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment on a baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating and compare its wear performance under incremental loads from room temperature to 800–900 °C against an as-deposited control
decision.why: The testable hypothesis is that the formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer dominates high-temperature wear resistance by minimizing abrasive or adhesive contact. Prior studies (e.g., PMC7515071) showed that oxide scale or spinel formation can enhance wear resistance at elevated temperatures; observing improved performance in the pre-oxidized coating (versus the baseline) would confirm this mechanism. If no differences in wear track morphology, friction coefficient, or wear rate emerge despite the pre-oxidation, it would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
